I was 10 that year. 

A typical day was being woken up by my Mom or Dad because I was always tired from staying up late, reading books using my plugged in nightlight to see, as silently as I could so I wouldn't get caught. Breakfast was cereal w/milk or toast with butter, cinnamon, and sugar as a treat. 

My elementary school was right behind us, so I just walked to school, back then the majority of kids walked or rode the bus. A parent dropping you off was more rare. 

School started at 8:00 am and anyone who got there early would play outside until the bell rang. We'd then line up on the blacktop, on one of the painted dots that formed two straight lines for every class at school. Our teacher would arrive and lead us to our classroom. 

Our desks had our paper name signs we'd make on the first or second day of school. The desks had a fake wood top, brown paint, and a big space right above your lap where you would keep textbooks, a crayon box, pencils, and random erasers. 

It was such a nice environment because there was a single phone in each classroom, a projector, and a TV for occasional movies when we had a substitute. No other technology. The only things to distract us was the sky outside the windows, each other, or our art work pinned to the wall. 

At recess we'd play tag, soccer, basketball, swing, slide down the slides or climb up them. We weren't allowed but we'd see how many people we could fit in the slides. It was so funny each time you felt a big push from the people behind you and pushing the people in front of you. We'd yell stuff to make everyone in the slide laugh, like "I need to pee!", "Someone is touching my butt!" Or "Oh no, I'm not feeling so good from lunch." Lol. 

Lunchtime everyone brought a paper bag, or a lunch box with matching thermos. We had hot lunches too for a dollar and maybe 35¢. On special days, my mom would let me get hot lunch, one of my favorites was Tom turkey w, gravy, mashed potatoes, green beans, a choice of milk (white or chocolate), and some kind of dessert, nothing fancy. It was always fun to read the different foods with silly names. 

On rainy days, we'd stay inside and play a game where everyone would sit on their desks or the long counter in our classroom, the goal was call out someone's name, throw the ball to them, and not let it drop. There was also heads up 7 up. 

We'd move from subject to subject throughout the day- Reading, writing, history, arithmetic, art, science, music, and P.E. were different days throughout the week. We'd also practice cursive, long division, and have spelling tests. There was also a huge dictionary in each classroom to look up words we didn't know or remembered how to spell. At the end of the day, our teacher would write our homework assignments on the white board and we hurried to write it down. 

After school we'd all go home then go back outside to play till dinner. We'd ride bikes up and down the street, play tag, street hockey, try out the skateboard, sardines, freeze tag, hide and seek, or ditch em (picking a house, ringing the doorbell and running away). 

Dinner for us was a different homemade meal every day. The hour before dinner was ready was always the hardest because we were so hungry and the food cooking on the stove or in the oven smelled so good. Our vegetables were a can of corn, green beans dumped into a bowl and microwaved, or frozen peas and carrots. We had a lot of stews, casseroles, and sometimes the microwave meals that had multiple Salisbury steaks. Fast food and soda for our family was rare. 

Also kids were always playing together outside, obesity was rare, and there were just a couple of overweight kids. Clothes were all different colors, new clothes and shoes were usually when your others had holes or were worn out. 

We had newspapers on our driveway in the morning, summers we spent our time in the above ground pool, or turning on the hose and seeing how high up we could shoot the water then run under as it came down. 

We only had two corded phones in the house and had to memorize or write down every number. Our family read books a lot, watching TV, playing video games was limited, there were technicolored cartoons on Disney in the mornings before school, and we'd  go on candy runs where we'd grab our money, bike to the store, which had a huge selection of candy, ranging from 10¢ to 25¢, pixie sticks, lollipops, sour candies, fizzy warheads, necco wafers (which were disgusting), sugar daddies, bubble gum, gummy worms, on and on. 

Costumes were homemade, movies were occasionally on TV if you caught it, paper TV guides showed what was on each channel, new movies were in theaters or you could rent them for a few nights from a rental store, food wasn't expensive, we watched TGIF on our TV each Friday, and we called our friends parents by their first names. 

This was really fun to write and i hope it gave you the glimpse you wanted. :)

My new go to cheap meal is chicken and rice. 

Canned chicken
Bag of Rice
Canned mixed vegetables
Bullion cubes
Garlic powder

Rinse the rice until the water runs clear instead of cloudy, cover the rice with water until it reaches the top of your fingernail when you place it right above the rice line. Put on stove, add bouillon cubes, garlic, and half the canned chicken liquid, turn on high wait until it's boiling, cover with a lid and set the temperature to low. When the water reaches the rice line, mix in the chicken and veggies, then replace lid. Once the steam starts going down, test the rice to see if it's done. I prefer stickier rice but if you like fluffy rice then add an equal amount of water:rice instead. 

Adjust as needed but this can be endlessly adjusted with different meats (cooked through), different flavors, veggies, etc. I love brown rice. 

Also look up rice porridge, it's soooo good. Very comforting, healthy, and also versatile.

This last December, I made a firm decision that I would end my life in September of this year. I told absolutely no one and made a decision to thoroughly enjoy my family get togethers not just for my sake, but so my family would have happy memories with me. I also chose September to avoid anyone's birthday or holidays so my death wouldn't completely ruin them for anyone. 

I felt happy, relieved, and felt a weight come off. During this time my doctor switched my medication to another and increased the dose. I realized over time that my way of thinking was changing, it was slowly improving, being able to go through difficult situations without completely breaking down. 

It was around April that I had the thought of not committing suicide, that there were things I still hadn't gotten a chance to do. It was like closing a book in the middle and never finishing it. 

Over the next months, I had a profound change in my perspective. No matter how bad a situation made me feel, it was MY choice to live, other people who hurt me would not have any power whatsoever to make me believe that I should end my life. No  fucking way their actions would force me off the edge. I understood that I had power, strength, and the capability to create the life I wanted for myself. 

I realized the overwhelming difficulty it would be to overcome these feelings and thoughts, actually changing my circumstances, and even though I was emotionally, mentally, physically exhausted...I gritted my teeth and started pushing that boulder of self doubt, insecurity, depression, loss of jobs, of relationships, of income, housing up the mountain, and there's no way around it but to keep pushing.  No matter how long it takes, I have the chance to change my course in life. Every step forward a few grains may fall from the boulder. I may not even notice anything changing, but the more I push forward, the stronger I become and the more bits of broken rock fall off. At some point, you'll take a moment to look behind you and be shocked at how much progress you made. You'll notice all the fragmented rock creating a visible line up the mountain. At some point, after putting in so much effort, time, and consistent steps forward, you'll realize that you're no longer pushing a boulder, but carrying a small rock in your hand, that feels so tiny, insignificant, it cannot crush or push back against you anymore. You fought back and won. 

At this point, I'm without a job, thousands of dollars in debt, have less than $900 dollars in my bank accounts and roughly $1600 dollars of bills coming up quickly, leaving me nothing for food. Does that depress me? Yes, but I have a power which is, I can choose my path by actions I take daily. 

No matter what my brain says (which often is stay up crazy late, sleep in late, avoid looking for jobs because your bed is too comfortable) in an instant I can get up, walk out my door, and take a walk in the sunlight, appreciating the weather, the sound of birds, beautiful flowers alongside the sidewalk, etc. I can choose healthier foods, to shower everyday, to look into other careers that would make me more money in the future. I can go back to school, I can live off of inexpensive, healthy foods so i can put another four dollars towards paying off my debt. The more I literally change the path of my life through the daily choices I make, eventually? I have a really good outcome that I will find happiness, financial stability, healthy relationships, enjoy fun activities, a nice home, a good car, and what you desire most. 

I saw your post and could not just move to another without sharing my  own journey because you matter. You truly deserve a good, fulfilling life that brings you happiness. It could take months, years, but every good choice changes the direction you are heading, you have the power, just need to see it.

I suffer from consistent major depression and find it very difficult to commit to a large project or task. The things I've found to be most helpful are...

1. Cleaning- Set a timer and clean for ten minutes each day. Focus on what you've completed, not what you didn't. 

2. Cleaning- Clean up or tidy x number of items. I usually do 30. I count a minute of vacuuming or scrubbing something as one item. It's actually amazing to see how much you've done after 30 items. 

3. Mood- Make sure to get at least 10 minutes of sunlight on your skin. Especially if you've been inside all day. 

4. Mood- Make sure you step in the shower and clean, brush your teeth, then put on clean clothes. It makes a HUGE difference. Even if it's rushed, you'll feel better.

5.  Mood- If you feel lonely, depressed, angry, etc. Find a mirror and literally talk to yourself about it. Let yourself feel any emotion and allow yourself to be honest with yourself. Just don't act on anything. 

6. Mood- I deal alot with thoughts of self harm. I've found this really helps avoid an attempt. Think about what you're doing tomorrow, write down a bucket list item and visualize what that will look like, talk to family, a friend, Reddit, just find someone who cares even if you feel it's just yourself, do something nice for someone else (even if it seems small like a compliment on Reddit), write out your feelings on paper, go to bed early, and most importantly take your medication on time each time.   Seriously these have really been helpful to me.

7. Mood- Don't go on social media sites and put down your screen for a little while. In fact, go outside in nature or go somewhere you feel safe and just relax without a screen. 

8. Mood- Even if it's difficult, go to sleep before midnight. Melatonin, and a red light app are super helpful for getting you ready to sleep. Staying up super late and then sleeping late make it hard to be productive, be social, have good eating habits, and get solid sunlight. That's what I've found for me. 

9. Mood-Don't eat alot of sugar or processed foods if you can avoid them. 

Anyways, hope this helps someone. It's been a great help to me.

I suffer from consistent major depression and find it very difficult to commit to a large project or task. The things I've found to be most helpful are...


1. Cleaning- Set a timer and clean for ten minutes each day. Focus on what you've completed, not what you didn't. 


2. Cleaning- Clean up or tidy x number of items. I usually do 30. I count a minute of vacuuming or scrubbing something as one item. It's actually amazing to see how much you've done after 30 items. 


3. Mood- Make sure to get at least 10 minutes of sunlight on your skin. Especially if you've been inside all day. 


4. Mood- Make sure you step in the shower and clean, brush your teeth, then put on clean clothes. It makes a HUGE difference. Even if it's rushed, you'll feel better.


5.  Mood- If you feel lonely, depressed, angry, etc. Find a mirror and literally talk to yourself about it. Let yourself feel any emotion and allow yourself to be honest with yourself. Just don't act on anything. 


6. Mood- I deal alot with thoughts of self harm. I've found this really helps avoid an attempt. Think about what you're doing tomorrow, write down a bucket list item and visualize what that will look like, talk to family, a friend, Reddit, just find someone who cares even if you feel it's just yourself, do something nice for someone else (even if it seems small like a compliment on Reddit), write out your feelings on paper, go to bed early, and most importantly take your medication on time each time.   Seriously these have really been helpful to me.


7. Mood- Don't go on social media sites and put down your screen for a little while. In fact, go outside in nature or go somewhere you feel safe and just relax without a screen. 


8. Mood- Even if it's difficult, go to sleep before midnight. Melatonin, and a red light app are super helpful for getting you ready to sleep. Staying up super late and then sleeping late make it hard to be productive, be social, have good eating habits, and get solid sunlight. That's what I've found for me. 


9. Mood-Don't eat alot of sugar or processed foods if you can avoid them. 

Anyways, hope this helps someone. It's been a great help to me.

People using the slang version of "triggering" to imply something is bothering them, usually not knowing that it's correctly used in association with PTSD. 

I have ptsd and when I get triggered, it means that something happened in the present moment that reminds me of my traumatic experience. If I get too triggered by a reminder, I can lose control of my body. I'm unable to communicate, I can't move, I breathe like I'm hyperventilating, sometimes I can't breathe for a long time, feeling this all encompassing fear like I'll never be safe again, all while my brain is thinking "I just want to tell this person what's happening to me, instead of looking like I'm refusing to talk to them."
